standard.title: Australia-Asia Trade
standard.description: the reasons Australia trades with other nations, and the patterns of trade between Australia and Asia
standard.prior_knowledge: From AC9HE9K02 (direct predecessor): how economic decision-making involves interdependence of consumers, businesses, financial sector and government, including globalisation and supply chains. From AC9HE9K01: Australia's financial sector and its global role. Students understand economic interdependence but have not yet specifically investigated why countries trade or analysed Australia's trade relationship with Asia.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students explain the reasons Australia trades with other nations and the patterns of trade between Australia and Asia.

nodes.label: Why countries trade
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can explain the reasons countries trade, including resource variations, comparative advantage, surplus goods and specialist goods.
nodes.minimum_width: Explain two reasons why countries trade (e.g. variations in resource availability and the ability to sell surplus production).
nodes.typical_width: Explain the full range of reasons countries trade: variations in quantity and quality of economic resources within and between countries; ability to sell surplus goods and services; need to buy goods and services not produced domestically; comparative advantage (specialising in what they produce most efficiently). Use concrete examples for each reason.
wider: Examine comparative advantage theory through a concrete bilateral example (e.g. Australia-Japan trade) and explain how specialisation creates mutual benefit even when one country could produce both goods
Investigate how trade agreements (e.g. ASEAN-Australia-NZ FTA, ChAFTA) reduce barriers to trade and explain how they change the reasons and incentives for trading
Analyse how non-economic reasons for trade (diplomatic relationships, national security, cultural exchange) interact with economic reasons in shaping Australia's trade partnerships
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who understand trade only as 'buying what you can't make' will be unable to analyse Australia's trade patterns in subsequent nodes — many Australian exports (iron ore, coal, education) are sold to countries that could obtain alternatives, making the resource-advantage and surplus explanations essential for accurate pattern analysis.

response_modes.reason: Trade reasons are often conflated by students (especially comparative advantage, which is counterintuitive). A structured framework — resource difference → specialisation → mutual benefit — helps students reason about why trade creates gains rather than treating it as a zero-sum exchange.

success_criteria: Explains at least two distinct reasons why countries trade
Uses a concrete example to illustrate each reason
Uses terms such as 'specialisation', 'comparative advantage', 'resources' correctly

nodes.label: Benefits of trade
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can identify and explain the economic, individual, business and national benefits of trade for Australia.
nodes.minimum_width: Identify and explain two benefits of trade — one economic benefit (e.g. increased production or household income) and one national or individual benefit.
nodes.typical_width: Explain the full range of trade benefits across the elaboration categories: economic benefits (increased production, specialisation, increased household incomes, increased employment); benefits for individuals and businesses (opportunities to sell surpluses, competition encouraging greater choice, connections for inventors and entrepreneurs with future discoveries); and national benefits (relationships between countries, access to health and education services, diversified sources of national income). Use Australian examples for each category.
wider: Evaluate the distribution of trade benefits within Australia — examining which industries, regions and demographic groups gain most from trade liberalisation and which may be disadvantaged
Investigate how services trade (education, tourism, financial services) creates benefits for Australia that differ in nature from goods trade benefits
Examine how Indigenous-owned businesses in Australia participate in trade (domestic and international) and what barriers or opportunities shape their experience of trade benefits

response_modes.reason: Students need examples across all three benefit categories (economic, individual/business, national) to address descriptor-level tasks. Systematically building the repertoire with Australian examples before analysis tasks prevents students from relying on one category only.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: The distribution of trade benefits across industries, regions and communities — including Indigenous businesses — provides rich analytical contexts that complicate the 'trade is good for everyone' simplification and build economic reasoning sophistication.
success_criteria: Identifies benefits of trade from at least two categories (economic, individual/business, national)
Explains each benefit with reference to an Australian example
Distinguishes between different types of trade benefits rather than listing them as equivalent

nodes.label: Patterns of Australia-Asia trade
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can analyse patterns of trade between Australia and Asian countries over time, including total value, composition and direction of trade.
nodes.minimum_width: Describe the current direction of trade between Australia and one Asian country (what Australia exports and imports) and identify one trend in this relationship over the past decade.
nodes.typical_width: Analyse patterns of trade between Australia and the countries of Asia over time using the elaboration dimensions: total value of trade each year; composition of trade (category of goods and services — resources, agricultural products, manufactured goods, services); direction of trade (exports to which countries, imports from which countries); and percentage change over a decade. Identify trends and changes in these patterns.
wider: Compare Australia's trade composition with Asia now versus 50 years ago, explaining what the shifts in composition reveal about changes in comparative advantage and economic development
Investigate the growth of services trade between Australia and Asia (education, tourism, financial services) alongside goods trade, and explain why services have grown as a share of the total

Analyse how China's economic development has changed its role in Australia's trade patterns — from a smaller trading partner to Australia's largest — and explain the economic factors driving this shift
nodes.hinge_reason: Analysing trade patterns requires being able to read multi-variable data (value, composition, direction, time) simultaneously. Students who cannot disaggregate pattern dimensions cannot address the analytical tasks in AC9HE9S03, which uses Australia-Asia trade as a primary example context.

response_modes.reason: Trade pattern analysis involves multiple simultaneous variables (value, composition, direction, change over time). A structured data-reading framework — what is traded, with whom, how much, how has this changed — prevents students from treating pattern analysis as a single-variable description.

Different Asian trading partners (China, Japan, South Korea, India, ASEAN) show different pattern characteristics. Using multiple partner contexts reveals the variation within 'Australia-Asia trade' and builds more accurate pattern understanding.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: Australia's trade relationship with Asia is dynamic and historically significant. The shift from primary partner UK to Asia, the rise of China, the growth of services — these are rich empirical patterns that connect to contemporary geopolitical and economic contexts students encounter in media.
success_criteria: Identifies the composition and direction of trade between Australia and at least one Asian country
Describes at least one trend in Australia-Asia trade patterns over time
Uses trade data vocabulary (exports, imports, total value, composition, direction)

nodes.label: Similarities, differences and interdependence in Australia-Asia trade
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can identify similarities and differences in Australia-Asia trade patterns over time and explain the interdependent nature of this trade relationship.
nodes.minimum_width: Identify one similarity and one difference in Australia's trade relationship with Asia now compared with 50 years ago, and explain one way the relationship is interdependent.
nodes.typical_width: Identify similarities and differences or trends in the composition and direction of trade between Australia and Asia now and 50 years ago (e.g. what goods/services have remained dominant, what has changed, which partners have risen or fallen in importance). Explain the interdependent nature of Australia-Asia trade — how Australian producers depend on Asian markets and Asian economies depend on Australian resources, commodities and services.
wider: Investigate how Australia's economic dependence on Asian demand for resources creates vulnerability — using a specific commodity and examining the consequences of demand fluctuation for Australian industries and regions
Examine the interdependence between Australian universities and international student income from Asian countries, analysing how COVID-19 border closures exposed this dependency
Analyse how new trade corridors (e.g. India, Vietnam, Indonesia) are diversifying Australia's trade interdependence and explain what is driving these shifts

response_modes.reason: This node integrates reasons for trade (Node 1), benefits of trade (Node 2), and pattern analysis (Node 3) into an explanation of the Australia-Asia interdependence. Students should connect: why trade exists → what patterns have developed → how these create mutual dependence.

success_criteria: Identifies at least one similarity and one difference in Australia-Asia trade patterns across different time periods
Explains how both Australia and Asian trading partners are interdependent in the trade relationship
Connects trade patterns to the underlying economic reasons for the relationship
